Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: JD is a well-known number-two or number-three player in a maturing Chinese e-commerce market, not the leader of an emerging industry, and its ADS fell about 16% over the past year. It lacks most Rule Breaker traits such as top-dog status in a new industry, strong momentum and a perception of being overvalued.
summaries.buffett: JD is understandable and conservatively financed, with RMB221.7 billion of cash and short-term investments against RMB69.9 billion of debt at June 30, 2026, and it trades around 1.1 times book. But its moat has not produced pricing power, returns on capital are low (2025 net margin 1.5%), and retained earnings have not built shareholder value over the past five years.
summaries.munger: Munger would value JD's hard-to-copy logistics network and founder control, but would worry that it competes in a brutal, price-driven industry where Alibaba, PDD, Douyin and Meituan keep rivals' margins thin. Inverting, there are several ways to disappoint: food-delivery losses, subsidy fade, Chinese regulation and US-China tensions.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms JD is a large stalwart with a turnaround angle: earnings fell in 2025 because of food-delivery losses and analysts expect a strong rebound, putting the forward P/E near 6.6 against forecast EPS growth of about 25% a year. It is not overlooked (around 37 analysts cover it), but the company is shrinking its share count through buybacks.
summaries.fisher: JD keeps opening new lines (logistics for third parties, JD Health, industrial procurement, food delivery, Europe) and has a strong sales and fulfilment organisation. Its very low profit margins (operating margin 0.2% in 2025) and modest return on research spending fall short of Fisher's emphasis on above-average margins.
summaries.graham: On Graham's numbers JD looks cheap: about 1.1 times book, P/E times P/B near 21 and roughly 8-9 times three-year average earnings, with ample net cash. It fails the defensive investor's record tests, however: it lost money in 2021 and earlier years and has paid dividends only since 2023.
summaries.thiel: JD has no technology ten times better than rivals and operates in a crowded market where competitors copy each other's moves, the opposite of Thiel's monopoly ideal. Its strongest answers are distribution and durability: a nationwide same/next-day logistics network built over two decades.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's discipline asks for durable growth, efficiency and attractive prices. JD is cheap on forward earnings (about 6.6 times) and free cash flow (yield about 12%), but growth has slowed to low single digits in 2026 and management chose to spend heavily on a food-delivery war, the opposite of getting fit.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and liquidity tailwinds. JD's earnings are expected to recover as food-delivery losses narrow (New Businesses loss cut to RMB9.9 billion in Q2 2026 from RMB14.8 billion), but revenue fell 2.9% that quarter and the share price trend is negative, so the setup is mixed at best.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high gross margins and cash conversion. JD fails on these: gross margin about 16%, return on invested capital around 1% and 2025 free cash flow of only RMB6.5 billion against RMB19.6 billion of net income.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula ranks companies on earnings yield and return on capital. JD's enterprise value is small relative to its sales because of large net cash, but trailing operating income is tiny (EV/EBIT about 41) and return on capital is low, so it would not rank well today.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, talented and honest management, and the ability to reinvest at high returns. JD has competent founder-controlled management but a low-return business, so the first and third legs are weak.
summaries.pabrai: JD fits parts of Pabrai's Dhandho approach: a simple business trading cheaply with large net cash, in a temporarily distressed setting (price war and food-delivery losses). The uncertainty is high and the downside is not as limited as Pabrai prefers, given Chinese regulatory and geopolitical risk.
summaries.wood: JD is a logistics-heavy retailer with some robotics and autonomous delivery, but it is not a leader in ARK's innovation platforms and its market is not set to multiply in size. It is a poor fit for Wood's disruptive-innovation approach.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and high barriers to entry. JD is simple and cheap but its cash flow is volatile, it is not dominant overall, and its results depend heavily on Chinese consumer conditions and policy.
summaries.sleep: JD does share savings with customers through low prices and fast free delivery, echoing Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model seen at Costco and Amazon. But its scale advantage has not translated into a clearly widening lead against PDD, Alibaba and Douyin.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products solving painful problems. JD solved a real problem in China (trusted goods delivered quickly), but today it is a mature incumbent rather than an early company riding a new technology wave.
summaries.nash: JD fails several of Nash's hard filters: it is a Chinese company, revenue growth is below 10%, operating margin is far below 20%, and margins have declined. It does pass on cash exceeding debt, a low valuation (forward PEG about 0.3) and recent earnings beats, scoring about 50 on his 13-category scorecard.

momentum.evidence: JD's ADS price was about $26.57 in mid-October 2026, down about 16% over the prior 52 weeks while the US market rose.

g4.evidence: Founder Richard Liu controls JD as chairman and Tencent is a long-standing strategic shareholder, but Walmart sold its stake in 2024 and CEO Sandy Xu is a professional manager rather than a celebrated leader.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly call JD cheap, with a consensus Strong Buy rating, an average price target of about $39 and a forward P/E near 6.6.

simple.evidence: JD mainly buys goods and resells them online in China, delivering them with its own logistics network, which a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue grew every year from RMB745.8 billion (2020) to RMB1,309.1 billion (2025), but net income swung from RMB49.4 billion (2020) to a RMB3.6 billion loss (2021) and RMB19.6 billion (2025).

integrity.evidence: JD has started dividends (US$1.00 per ADS for 2025) and large buybacks, but founder Richard Liu holds majority voting control through dual-class shares, limiting outside shareholders' influence.

b6.evidence: JD entered a costly food-delivery war against Meituan and Alibaba in 2025, losing RMB46.6 billion in New Businesses that year, and is buying Ceconomy in Europe, which looks like expansion for its own sake to critics.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital was about 1% on a trailing basis and the 2025 operating margin was just 0.2%.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow exceeded net income in 2024 (RMB43.7 billion vs RMB41.4 billion), but in 2025 it was only RMB6.5 billion against RMB19.6 billion of net income.

b10.evidence: JD kept most of its earnings over the past five years, yet its market value fell to about US$36 billion in October 2026, well below its 2021 level.

safety.evidence: JD trades near 1.1 times book with roughly US$22 billion of net cash and short-term investments against a market value of about US$36 billion, a sizeable margin of safety if profits recover.

fairprice.evidence: At about 6.6 times forward earnings and a free-cash-flow yield near 12%, the price is low even for a low-growth, low-margin business.

mu5.evidence: JD could be hurt by a prolonged price and food-delivery war, fading subsidies, weak Chinese consumption, Chinese regulation and US-China tensions affecting its ADR listing.

reinvest.evidence: Its main reinvestment projects (food delivery, Europe) are loss-making so far, and core retail earns low single-digit margins.

ly2.evidence: JD fits as a stalwart turnaround: a large retailer whose profits should recover as food-delivery losses narrow, though the story depends on the outcome of the price war.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 6.6 is well below the roughly 25% annual EPS growth analysts forecast for the next three years, though the trailing P/E is about 18.7.

runway.evidence: Food delivery, logistics for outside customers, JD Health and Europe (Joybuy, MediaMarkt) offer new growth, but the core China retail market is maturing.

ly7.evidence: Diluted ADS equivalents fell from about 1,590 million in 2022 to 1,408 million in Q2 2026 through buybacks, but there is no record of notable insider open-market buying.

ly8.evidence: Chinese stocks are out of favour with many US investors, but JD is widely covered by about 37 analysts.

fi2.evidence: JD keeps launching new businesses, including JD Takeaway food delivery (2025), Joybuy in six European countries (March 2026) and autonomous delivery vehicles.

fi3.evidence: Its technology spending produced a highly automated logistics network and in-house AI models, but has not lifted margins meaningfully.

fi4.evidence: JD is strong at large shopping festivals (618 started as JD's anniversary sale) and electronics merchandising, but marketing-led rivals such as PDD and Douyin are growing faster.

longterm.evidence: Management accepted a fall in operating income from RMB38.7 billion (2024) to RMB2.8 billion (2025) to build food delivery and keeps investing in logistics and Europe.

gr1.evidence: JD had RMB1,309.1 billion (about US$187 billion) of revenue in 2025.

ni10.evidence: JD reported a net loss of RMB3.6 billion in 2021 and also lost money in the mid-2010s.

gr4.evidence: JD only began paying annual cash dividends in 2023 (for fiscal 2022).

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS was RMB12.90 per ADS in 2025 versus a loss in 2015, so it has improved, but growth from a loss base cannot be measured as a percentage.

gr6.evidence: Average net income for 2023-2025 was about RMB28.4 billion (about US$4.2 billion), so a US$36 billion market value is roughly 8-9 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: With a trailing P/E near 18.7 and price/book near 1.13, the product is about 21, just under Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: JD's logistics and technology are strong but not ten times better than rivals such as Cainiao, SF Express and Meituan's delivery network.

timing.evidence: Chinese consumer weakness and fading trade-in subsidies hurt timing in 2026, though food-delivery losses are narrowing.

th3.evidence: JD started by dominating online sales of electronics in China and expanded into general merchandise, but it never became the overall market leader.

team.evidence: Founder Richard Liu built JD into China's largest retailer by revenue and remains chairman, but CEO Sandy Xu is a finance professional with a short record as CEO since 2023.

th5.evidence: JD owns its distribution: an app used by hundreds of millions of Chinese shoppers and a nationwide delivery network that reaches them directly.

durable.evidence: Its logistics network should stay valuable for decades, but shopping habits have shifted quickly to PDD and Douyin, showing China e-commerce share is not secure.

th7.evidence: JD's current bets (food delivery, Europe) enter markets already led by Meituan and Amazon rather than unseen opportunities.

trend.evidence: JD is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud; it is a retailer and logistics operator in a maturing market.

dr1.evidence: Q2 2026 net income rose 15.4% to RMB7.1 billion and JD beat EPS estimates in each of the last four quarters, but revenue fell 2.9%.

dr2.evidence: If food-delivery losses keep narrowing and Ceconomy is consolidated, JD could look better in two years, but sales growth and subsidy fade are uncertain.

dr4.evidence: Low Chinese interest rates and stimulus help, but deflation, weak consumer confidence and fading appliance trade-in subsidies work against it.

dr6.evidence: Narrowing food-delivery losses, closing of the Ceconomy deal, ongoing buybacks (US$1.0 billion in H1 2026) and the November Singles' Day season could lift results.

dr7.evidence: Chinese regulatory and geopolitical risks and a price war make JD hard to justify as a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was about 16.0% in 2025, typical of a first-party retailer and not a sign of pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: The trailing free-cash-flow yield is about 12%, though 2025 free cash flow (RMB6.5 billion) was well below 2024's RMB43.7 billion.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income is small relative to enterprise value, with EV/EBIT around 41.

pa2.evidence: The 2025 profit collapse came mainly from food-delivery subsidies (New Businesses loss of RMB46.6 billion), which management can scale back, and losses already narrowed in Q2 2026.

pa4.evidence: Net cash of about RMB152 billion and RMB282 billion of equity cushion the downside, but Chinese policy and ADR-delisting risks could cause permanent loss.

wo1.evidence: JD uses warehouse robots and autonomous delivery vehicles and has its own AI models, but it is not a leader in AI or robotics.

wo2.evidence: Logistics unit costs fall with volume, but this is a mature process, not a fast cost decline unlocking huge new demand.

wo3.evidence: JD combines retail, logistics and some AI and robotics, but not several ARK-style innovation platforms at scale.

wo4.evidence: China online retail and food delivery are large but not set to grow many times in five years.

ac3.evidence: JD is not a commodity producer, but its results depend on Chinese consumer spending, government subsidies and fuel and labour costs for delivery.

ns1.evidence: JD passes scale savings to customers through low prices and free fast delivery, but rivals with lighter models undercut it on price.

ns4.evidence: Whether JD's food delivery and European expansion strengthen its position in 10-20 years is still unclear.

va2.evidence: JD solved the painful problem of fake goods and slow delivery in Chinese e-commerce, but that problem is now largely solved across the industry.

tn1.evidence: JD sells into the maturing e-commerce market rather than a new secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market prices JD as a low-margin Chinese retailer, while it is also becoming a logistics, food-delivery and European omnichannel retailer, though these are not yet profitable.

tn3.evidence: JD is a Chinese company, one of Nash's zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025, JD was profitable in 2025 (net income RMB19.6 billion), and it held RMB221.7 billion of cash and short-term investments against RMB69.9 billion of debt at June 30, 2026.

tn5.evidence: Cash exceeded debt in each recent quarter, but quarter-by-quarter free cash flow is not verified here; full-year 2025 free cash flow was positive at RMB6.5 billion.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 13.0% in 2025 but fell 2.9% in Q2 2026, and the 2026 consensus is about 3% growth.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 13.0% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 0.5% gives about 13.5, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue rose 13.0% but operating income fell from RMB38.7 billion to RMB2.8 billion, so costs grew faster than revenue.

tn9.evidence: JD's operating margin is far below 20% (0.2% in 2025) and revenue growth is below 10% in 2026.

tn10.evidence: JD faces Chinese platform and pricing regulation, scrutiny of the food-delivery subsidy war, and US-China risks to its ADR listing.

tn11.evidence: JD provides genuine goods delivered same or next day that help Chinese shoppers buy with confidence, and earns money mainly from the retail margin on goods it sells plus logistics, marketplace and ad fees.

tn13.evidence: Total about 50: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 0, operating margin 0, short interest 10, institutional ownership 5, revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 5, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year and cash exceeded debt, but operating margin fell from 1.7% (2020) to 0.2% (2025) and free cash flow fell from RMB34.9 billion to RMB6.5 billion.

tn15.evidence: Trailing interest coverage is below 1x on reported operating income, even though the current ratio is about 1.1 and liabilities are well under 4 times equity.

tn18.evidence: CEO Sandy Xu has been in the role only since May 2023, is not the founder and has no record of open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: JD beat consensus adjusted EPS estimates in each of the last four quarters, Q3 2025 to Q2 2026.

tn21.evidence: Operating margin has declined sharply (from 3.3% in 2024 to 0.2% in 2025) and JD is making a large acquisition of Ceconomy.

tn22.evidence: JD has over RMB1.3 trillion of revenue, is profitable and buys back shares rather than issuing them.

tn24.evidence: At an enterprise value of about US$13 billion against about US$187 billion of revenue, the price implies little or no growth, below the 13% JD delivered in 2025.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year averages (growth about 7.8%, FCF margin about 2.7%), 5 years of FCF, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate plus RMB152 billion net cash gives roughly US$70 per ADS, above the $26.57 price.

tn26.evidence: The forward P/E of about 6.6 against forecast EPS growth of about 25% gives a PEG near 0.3, cheap versus peers like Alibaba.
